You think your phone knows where you are.
It doesn't. It only listens to clocks.
Let those clocks slip, and GPS drifts eleven kilometres a day.
In 1973, the Pentagon approved a satellite navigation network. By 1995, it was fully operational.
It has three parts. Satellites in orbit. Ground stations that watch them. And the receiver in your pocket.

Each satellite broadcasts the exact time it sent its signal. Your phone compares that with its own clock. Light covers three hundred thousand kilometres a second, so the delay gives your distance. Four satellites pin you down.
But one millionth of a second of error is three hundred metres.
And the satellites zip along at fourteen thousand kilometres an hour, so Einstein says their clocks run slow. But weaker gravity speeds them up even more.
Net result: thirty-eight microseconds fast, every day.
So engineers detune the clocks before launch, slow on the ground, and exactly right in space.
Your phone doesn't find you. Einstein does.
Would you trust a map that ignored relativity?
